title: AI Governance for Legal SMEs: EU AI Act Compliance for Law Firms
author: Dr. Hernani Costa
summary_short: European law firms face a three-layer AI compliance framework: GDPR, EU AI Act, and professional conduct rules. Unlike other sectors, legal work involves attorney-client privilege that sits above EU AI Act obligations. Contract review AI tools aren't high-risk under the Act, but firms must manage data processing agreements, confidentiality safeguards, and human oversight requirements.
summary_medium: This article outlines a three-layer AI governance framework for European law firms navigating EU AI Act compliance, specifically designed for 15-25 person practices. The first layer is GDPR, requiring data processing agreements with AI vendors, data subject rights compliance, and special category data handling for matters involving health, political, or criminal data. The second layer involves EU AI Act deployer obligations: document system purpose, maintain human oversight, and keep usage records. Crucially, contract review and legal research tools used by private firms fall outside the Act's high-risk categories, which target AI used in judicial proceedings by public authorities. The third layer, often omitted from generic compliance guides, is professional conduct: bar association rules on confidentiality, attorney-client privilege, and the requirement that lawyers maintain independent professional judgment over AI-generated work product. The article recommends a phased implementation: inventory tools in weeks one through two, close gaps in weeks three through five, and establish a quarterly governance review cycle. Firms should consult their bar association and professional indemnity insurer before processing privileged material through external AI APIs.
summary_long: This article provides a comprehensive three-layer AI governance framework for European law firms implementing EU AI Act compliance, tailored specifically for small to mid-sized practices of 15 to 25 attorneys. The framework recognizes that legal services face unique compliance challenges arising from the inherent sensitivity of client data, which simultaneously constitutes personal data under GDPR, commercially sensitive information under contractual confidentiality terms, and potentially privileged material under attorney-client privilege doctrine. The first compliance layer addresses GDPR obligations, requiring law firms as data controllers to execute data processing agreements with every AI vendor processing client personal data. These agreements must specify purpose limitation preventing vendor use of client data for model training, establish data retention limits, define deletion obligations, and guarantee EEA processing where applicable. Firms must also ensure their privacy notices disclose AI processing and maintain capability to retrieve and delete client data upon data subject request. Special category data under GDPR Article 9, including health data in personal injury cases, political opinions in employment matters, and criminal offence data in defence work, requires explicit consent or valid legal basis before AI processing, as standard vendor DPAs rarely cover these categories. The second layer covers EU AI Act deployment obligations. While the Act's Annex III lists high-risk AI categories relevant to legal work—including AI used in administration of justice under Annex III(8)—private law firm tools for contract review, document drafting, legal research, and case summarisation fall outside these high-risk classifications. The Act's general deployer obligations still apply: documenting AI system purpose and scope, implementing human oversight for all AI-assisted outputs, maintaining usage records per document retention policies, and monitoring for accuracy drift. The third and most distinctive layer addresses professional conduct rules that sit above both GDPR and EU AI Act requirements. Bar association rules in European jurisdictions obligate lawyers to exercise independent professional judgment and maintain client confidentiality. Whether using an AI tool that transmits client information through external APIs breaches confidentiality depends on whether the vendor functions as a subprocessor under a DPA or constitutes a disclosure requiring separate client consent. The Dutch Bar Association, German Bar Association, and French National Bar Council have all issued guidance on AI use by lawyers in recent years. Critically, lawyers remain personally responsible for work product delivered to clients: AI-generated contract clauses or legal opinions must be reviewed, edited, and approved by a qualified attorney before client delivery, aligning EU AI Act human oversight requirements with professional conduct obligations. The article recommends a three-phase implementation: inventory and classify existing AI tools in weeks one through two, close gaps by signing missing DPAs and consulting bar associations in weeks three through five, and establish an ongoing quarterly governance review rhythm to maintain compliance as tools and guidance evolve.
